A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 87
King Druzz of the Duergar shifted the haft of his axe. He was quietly confident, but he would be ready if the enemy did make it through.
   The axe was the Axe of the Dwarven Lords, and now it belonged in the Underdark. 
   Druzz was waiting at the end of a long wide  tunnel.  Marching feet and muffled voices echoed down from a distant branch. The king tensed, only a thin sheen of sweat signified any  nervousness.
   The sounds grew slightly louder, then louder.. the first ranks of Overlight dwur must be reaching the bend!
    Then the screaming started.
                    **************
   It had been five weeks, and the dwarven sortie sent into the Underdark to retrieve the Axe had not returned
.   Pious Grimm Quartztusk realised that he had failed. He knew that invading the Underdark would be perilous, but it still stung. More good lives had been lost.
 Unfortunately, there were even more pressing problems. Two of the escaped political prisoners, each a Moradinson and cousin to the late Silvervein, had gathered a large number of supporters around them. 
   The Crystalmist dwur were now divided. Many supported Pious, but with the Axe lost, a growing minority were of  the opinion that Silvervein had been a true king after all. 
   One of the Moradinson cousins (as Silvervein had left no heirs), it was suggested, should be appointed as a new king.
   O, Moradin, Return Great king! Return!
      Pious Grimm Quartztusk felt his head aching again. He poured himself a mop of fortified wine when a messenger ran into the chamber and urged him to get to the main gate.  Pious found a large group of duergar gathering there. They looked officious, wrapped in silver and bronze coloured capes. One carried a flag of truce. 
   Pious realised that they were waiting for him.. He quickly gathered his bodyguard and climbed the stairs to meet them.
   As he reached the gates, he saw that the duergar were all heavily armed and armoured underneath their capes. Would they attack? Pious paused a moment, but not one duergar attempted to force the gate. Pious moved on.
 One duergar, grey skinned like the others, but with unusually piebald hair, raised a hand in salute.
   "Hail, Pious Grimm, leader of the Crystalmist people," he said "I, Turiziz, Fane  of Great Bore, home of the great Duergar nation, Command thee to submit to our King, King of All, holder of the Fierce Axe,  King Druzz the Terrible!  Submit or die!" See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 88
   Pious Grimm Quartztusk was incredulous. This strange looking grey dwarf, Turiziz  (the 
 Fane of Bore, whatever that meant) was threatening the destruction of his people with such one band of troops. 
   Did they not understand their dwur kin? The Mountain dwarves of the Crystalmists were implacable on their own turf. Pious considered giving the signal to launch his Hammers upon the duergar rabble but...was he underestimating them?
   Corrupted they might be, but the duergar were still dwur. They had survived in darkness, bathed in Arcane radiation. And this "Fane" looked so calm, his eyes meeting his own with an even steadiness.
   Pious composed himself. He was the High Steward because he could make reasoned, considered decisions, unlike his predecessor, Silvervein.
   Unfortunately, even considered decisions could be bad ones.
   Finally Pious spoke.
   "I cannot seriously consider your proposal to submit. Your people have stolen the Fierce Axe, despite us offering you succour.  You should return it from the Underdark where you hid it, or...or we will rightly launch bloody vengeance upon thee."
   The Duergar emissary shrugged., his brilliant cape glowing in the moonlight.
   "WAR IT BE." he intoned, then Turiziz turned about and led his kin down the road and away from the city. Pious watched them disappear into the darkness.
                          *************
   Days went by and nothing more from the duergar was heard.  Meantime his hold on the Crystalmists was slipping. The Moradinson cousin, Ironcheek and Copperhelm,  had consolidated enough support to occupy their own sections of Grawn. 
To remove them now would be bloody, and that was not what Pious wanted. The two cousins were jostling for ascendency, but neither had turned to violence. Grawn was an angry, divided city,  full of robust debate and insult, a volcano gurgling and rumbling, but sleeping still.
   Pious Grimm Quartztusk ordered his palace to be further fortified, then worked with advisors on a new plan to retrieve the Fierce Axe. See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 89
   Three more missions were launched to wrest the Axe of the Dwarven Lords from the  Underdark.
     All three failed.  
   Orders were given to seal the cave openings, but the Underdark is vast, and there are always secret ways in and out.  
   Still,  no duergar army appeared on the scene to melee with the surface dwarves.  Pious Grimm Quartztusk was most concerned about the duergar living amongst them. They were an obvious danger if they still followed their king. If this was so, then their king would be foolish if he didn't use them.
   Pious wanted to banish them, force them into Western Oerik, but many were now integrated in ordinary dwur society. Some had married Crystalmist dwarves.  
   Pious had reached out to the two Moradinson factions, despite his belief that they were misguided fools. Many dwur followed one or the other, this was a reality. If he could gain agreement with them on at least the duergar issue, that would be one less headache.
   His head did ache. More than it had before. Pious fancied that the pounding was Moradin. Moradin was talking to him in a secret language, one that Pious as yet did not understand. Moradin was in trouble somehow.
   Somewhere.
   After taking another nip of brandy, he focused back upon reality, a reality that was heading towards another bloody war. See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 90
473 SD
   War engulfed the dwarf realms.
    Most accepted that the Axe was lost, probably forever.  There were even rumours that the duergar never stole it at all, that it was actually hidden by one of the other factions in order to deny the true ruler.
   The surface duergar themselves split into two opposing groups; those that stayed loyal to the duergar king and plotted for ultimate conquest of the surface dwellers, and those who liked the new lifestyle they had adopted.
   Blood flowed freely and few dwarves across Eastern Oerik could escape the turmoil.  There were neutrals who migrated to non- dwarven places like Blemu, and south of Celene, and some went to Sunndi where the grey elves were liberal and tolerant of all the good aligned races, but most dwur picked a side and were caught up in the ferocious battles.
   Pious Grimm Quartztusk led his most loyal Hammers against his misguided foes, delivering blow after blow.
    He never gave up announcing his considered and correct position. Only Moradin could be king.
   Night after night whether asleep in blankets on the side of a mountain, or tucked within the palace, the pounding of his head continued, just as his Hammers pounded his enemies.
   Moradin was calling him, but where was he, and why was he not communicating with his clerics praying continuously in the temples?
 Terrible stories had filtered down to him that the humanoids had launched a secret weapon on that distant world of Toril, and that Moradin and the elf god were mortally wounded or imprisoned and their armies crushed.  
   And throughout the fighting, the duergar king laid tucked away in the Underdark, waiting. See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 97
523 SD
   Duergar had lived in the hills south of the Suss forest for nearly sixty years.  The ongoing Dwarven Wars meant that reintegration with the surface dwarves was not possible, so they kept to themselves and maintained their old ways.
   The duergar spent most of their time underground, the terrain they knew best. They struggled to understand how the Overlight denizens could function in the middle of Summer. Down in the dark there were no Seasons.
   The duergar easily overcame and dominated the local goblins, xvarts, norkers and kobolds. The humanoids were then recruited and used for scouting, exploration, hunting and robbing.
 The duergar were satisfied with their cavernous lairs, but were disappointed to find no connection to the honeycomb of tunnels that led into the Underdark and their King.
This fact did not stop a hardy handful from investigating further. They dug new tunnels that bypassed rock falls, dead ends and water filled chasms.
   Eventually, a narrow shaft broke open into a musty, cold, network of complex caves. It was a new region of the Underdark, undisturbed for millennia. 
   There was no fungal luminescence upon the walls, there were no monsters, everything felt untouched. 
   Food and water would be a problem, so the duergar explorers organised camps to be established at strategic points. Likely, hard work would establish a new link to their homeland, then their empire could expand and seed these dead caves with life.
  After a few hours, the duergar struggled to concentrate. A  dread feeling touched their bones and made them weigh like lead, but the grey dwur were nothing if not stoic, and they pushed through.
   Ghimlit suddenly let out a cry of delight.He had  broken through a slab of rock that led him into a series of new caverns. Caverns made of gemstones.
   The duergar hurried through the hole and breathed in the beauty.
   Unfortunately, they were extremely close to danger. 
   Not far away lay the hitherto undisturbed resting place of the Undead Dragon... See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 98
-14,'000 SD
   Tiamat spawned the chromatic dragons in order to gain great power for herself.  Weaker than most other Grand Drakes, she hated her brethren and wished to rise above them all.
   The blue, black, white, green and red dragons were cowed and subdued by her. Bent to her will they submitted themselves to vile magical rituals that allowed Tiamat to grow an extra head, one for each of the chromatic types.  
   Tiamat proudly sported her new look, flaunting her Greatness. Bahamut, her brother, would finally recognise her as an equal, and she would no longer be shunted out from the Palace.
   but Bahamut, the Platinum dragon, and the greatest Grand Drake outside of Kara-Tur, continued to shun her. In fact, he seemed shocked and appalled. 
   "Do you not see the new me?" Asked Tiamat, " can you not see my new heads, my gathered power?"
Bahamut turned his face away from his sister, 
   "I saw it," answered Bahamut, "and I wish I had not. What price did your offspring pay for you to become this abomination?"
   Tiamat's eyes flashed, and her various heads glowered.
   "My offspring are mine to do with as I please."
   "No!" Snapped Bahamut, "no!" You will never understand our True Way, our True Purpose. Power is not won by exploiting others."
           ***********************
    Desperate to bring down her arrogant brother,  Tiamat bred further types.  The brown and yellow dragons fled from her rather than submit so she gained nothing from them. 
    Enraged, Tiamat flew upon each of the extant metallic dragons, the spawn of Bahamut.  One brass, bronze, copper, silver and electrum* dragon were each slain and their bones gathered together.  Their glands that allowed their breath weapon attacks were combined, powdered and sprinkled upon the bones.  Using Necromancy, the bones reanimated into a distorted skeleton of oddly miss-proportioned bones, each joint connected with ectoplasm. 
   What was Reborn became the first and most terrible Undead being that ever crawled upon the Oerth.  
                    *****************
   Tiamat had shackled the monster with Mighty Magicks. Tiamat would subdue it and take all of its Unnatural power. Then, Bahamut would be thrown down and Tiamat would be Empress!
 If she had succeeded in taming the monster, then Tiamat would certainly have taken over the Dragon Empire and the elves would have never inherited Oerth.  This did not happen. 
    The Undead Dragon merely sniffed at her bonds and they shattered.  She stared at Tiamat, sizing the multi headed dragon up. Then, with a ghastly groan, the Thing  breathed out a haunted blast of hate that sent Tiamat howling away.  
                    ******************
   This Undead Dragon roamed the Oerth for nearly a century before the Celestial Empire, led by Bahamut, managed to trap her underneath the low mountains of the Dranchensgrab. She was confined to a small area of the Underdark, sealed with magical traps, and undisturbed and forgotten, until the duergar arrived in 523 SD.
* Gold dragons are not true metallic dragons but are Kara-turan drakes who revere Bahamut (there were Occidental gold dragons, but they went their own way and are now presumed extinct). See less

A History of Oerik
Book 1 
Part 99
    Long had she slept.
     The duergar found the Undead Dragon slumbering atop a mighty mound of treasure.. 
    When the Grand Drakes entombed her in the Underdark, they appeased her with great gifts.  Without a horde her dragon nature would have become too unstable and nothing magical or otherwise could have held her back for long.
   The enormous misshapen skeleton lay over the treasure mound,  unaware of her interlopers.  Her minds' were in the Dream Realms, reminiscing over her lost lives, for she was a hideous reconstruction of several individuals put together by Tiamat.
    Once in a while a cloud of ghostly flame would emanate from her half open mouth and slowly turn to mist.  
   The duergar entered the cavern and immediately spied the slumbering pile of bones, articulated into the shape of a great dragon. They were torn between terror and Goldust.  Once they realised that the puffs of green flame were not at all aimed at them, that the dragon in fact seemed totally oblivious to their presence, they carefully made their way to the foot of the treasure horde.
   Gemstones there were, sapphires and diamonds and rubies and emeralds.  There was something odd about their look, their colour.  Somehow they had been changed by the close proximity to the Undead Dragon. 
    Each gemstone felt very cold as if they had been buried in ice.  And, despite their type, all the gems shone ghostly green in the dark.  
   The piles of gold and silver appeared dull and bleached,   yet the duergar KNEW that they were of great value just the same.  
   The duergar opened their magically large sacks and bags  and filled them with as much treasure as they could carry, being careful not to wake the massive skeletal thing creaking above them.  
   Too much power lay within the Undead Dragon, and too much time being confined in one place. 
    Her deathly flame breath had permeated the walls, the ceiling and the floor of the cavern.  Over time, like liquid limestone forming stalactites and stalagmites, the ghostly smoke, fire and mist had turned its very surroundings into Undeath.
 When the duergar turned and left,  Shadows silently crept after them... See less

The War of the Eight Houses (2)
   Jaspi noticed that the ska knew the way to the Neheli camp. What were ska's? They looked like ordinary people, ordinary Suel. Why was it forbidden to talk to them?
   "We clean the dead. We bury them," said the ska, "This makes us unclean. Don't you understand this?"
   Jaspi waved a hand in annoyance. What a strange culture, she thought. Thank Wee Jas that the Linth didn't divide people up like that. the two Suel finally saw ahead of them two wooden gates of a stockade. The camp. The girl stopped two hundred yards away. Jaspi tried to urge her forward, but the girl wouldn't budge.
   "Oh, right, you can't go on because you are untouchable."
   The girl nodded.
   "If you can't go into the camp, how did you know exactly where it was?"
   The girl explained that the ska provide important services by taking care of the dead. Periodically, the Neheli Suel leave food and water here.
   "You stay then," said Jaspi, "I'm going in. My daughter is in there."
                               ******
   Jaspi showed the Neheli sentries her mark of nobility. She was an important personage of the Linth house, a house currently neutral with the Neheli. They took her through to the commander. He wore bronze armour embellished with red feathers. Jaspi explained that she believed her daughter was here somewhere, captured in the battle. 
   "Why did your daughter breach our peace between houses?" asked the commander, "if she is our captive, then she must be a belligerent."
   Jaspi said that she didn't know. "Please, let me see her at least," she begged, "let me know that she is alive."
   The commander couldn't see the harm in that, so he asked Jaspi to wait in the tent with the guards whilst he made enquiries. After a short time he returned with a haughty young woman in manacles. It was Majeem her daughter!
   "Why have you come for me, mother?" said Majeem, "you have no honour. I would rather be here in chains than ever return with you."
. See less

Part 44
The War of the Eight Houses (3)
   Cenc was very afraid. She couldn't go back to her people because her dishonor of going with the strange woman couldn't be forgiven. She had only gone because she had been too scared to think straight. And, out there, on the plains, on the other side of the military camp, a bird was searching for prey. A large bird. A terrible bird. An axe beak, larger than a gnoll, who would run her down if it saw her. Cenc ducked down, her brown tunic and brown hair blending with the brown dirt. If only she had taken her noise maker to scare it off, but she had left it behind with everything else.
     The axe beak glanced in her direction, but it was still a long way off. Finally, it moved off into the shrubs. Cenc had scrunched her eyes as tightly as she could, willing herself to become invisible. Whether she had actually succeeded or not, she didn't know, but the danger was passed. Cenc decided to continue waiting. The woman might come back, and if not, in a few hours the gates would open and there would be food.
                                *****
     The commander had found the reunion between the mother and daughter rather amusing. It wasn't as if the captive was going to be released anyway, but the fact that the girl didn't want to go...now that was a chuckle. 
   The mother had visibly flinched at her daughter's words, and she watched the haughty girl being led back to the cell with a slump to her shoulders.
   The commander couldn't help himself. He patted her upper arm, "There, there, madam, every family has their little tiffs."
   Jaspi recoiled from his touch and her eyes flashed, "Who do you think you are? Commoner."
   The commander struck her across the face. "I run this camp. I am above everyone. I should have you killed, even if that means war with another house."
   Jaspi considered her options. Turn the commander into a lizard? Tempting, but it wouldn't help her or Majeem. She put her hands up in an attempt to placate him. "I am sorry, commander. I know that you are sovereign here. I am distressed."
   The commander nodded, "I accept your apology. Families are difficult."
   Jaspi flinched, but she held her temper. "What will you do with my daughter?" she asked.
   "She will be interrogated here, then, if she is of noble blood as you say, she will be taken back to our capital, and our emperor will keep her safe until a ransom is paid."
   Jaspi paused. The Neheli had an emperor? These ridiculous wars. How many Suel emperors were there now? Three, at least. It seemed that nearly every powerful house was trying to take over the Imperium. At least her Linth house hadn't joined in. Yet. The capture of Majeem might change things.
   "I have money with me," said Jaspi, "and I can quickly bring more. Let me pay you, and let me bring her home."
   The commander scowled, "I can't do that. That would be stealing from the emperor. I have been most patient with you, but you cannot stay here anymore. You must go."
                          *****
    It was dusk when Jaspi left the camp. The girl was gone.
   No, there she was, that strange ska girl. She was so small and so beige brown that in the darkening light, Jaspi nearly hadn't seen her at all. See less

The War of the Eight Houses (6)
   Cenc saw, high in the sky, a red dragon.
   Cenc was beside Jaspi on the ridge, unnoticed. Jaspi was her master, and Jaspi had forced her to come to watch the battle, but Cenc knew only too well what remained after a war.
   So she looked up, instead.
   The red dragon flew high, and fast, so Cenc could only glimpse a smear of colours as it sped across a clear patch between the clouds. And just for a second, Cenc had the impression that the dragon was being ridden by a rider, a black skeleton wielding a silver glinted sword.
   Cenc heard the muffled explosion, and involuntarily returned to the unfolding battle below.
   All the soldiers were dead.
                              *****
   Jaspi saw the golden chariot come down off the opposite ridge, make its way across the carnage, and then race towards her, horses sweating in the sunlight. Majeem was coming to see her.
   Jaspi waved to her daughter, then made her way down the jagged path to meet her.
   "Mother!" hissed Majeem, "How could you do this? They were our men too."
   Jaspi was startled. Did Majeem think that she had killed everyone? "It has nothing to do with me," she said, her voice raised, but Majeem cut her off.
   "Why the hell are you here then? Your magic has done this. I will kill you!" she drew her sword.
   Jaspi forced herself into stillness. She saw confusion and outrage reflected in her daughter's face. She felt the same way. Something terrible had happened. Jaspi muttered a couple of words and made out a circle with her arms. Majeem became as rigid as stone.
   "Hear me, daughter," said Jaspi tenderly to the  spellbound Majeem, "none of this was of my doing. I did come here for a reason. I was waiting for the fight to end." she waved one finger and Majeem gasped. Now she could speak.
   "What have you done to me? I cannot move!"
   "I will release you soon," said Jaspi, "now wait. I will turn you around. There. Watch the battlefield."
   A half hour went by. Another hour went by.  Then, suddenly, figures were moving amongst the dead, checking for life, digging pits.
   "They were here all the time," said Jaspi, "unnoticed and unloved even by that mysterious explosion. They are here to clean up, perhaps scrounge some food and coin." They are called the untouchables, the Ska. And, daughter, they are going to end the entire war." See less

Part 59
Religious Fervour in Silver Land
1710 SD
   The elves of Silver Land in north west Mystara had become very unruly. Lord Kint put down the latest report. Wasn't he a reasonable man? The elves wanted nice homes and nice food, so didn't it then make sense to do what you are told? Capricious, foolish creatures.
   Another crackdown was in order. Lord Kint went down a couple of flights of stairs then opened up the secret door behind the last step. The room beyond was tiny and pitch black, but Lord Kint was a lich, transformed by Vecna after some heart troubles, and darkness had no effect upon his vision. There was another concealed door in the far wall. This door opened up into what was little more than a secret shelf. And on the shelf was a jar. A jar that contained a heart. Lord Kint's old, mortal heart. Lord Kint pulled out the jar, then held it close to his cold, undead chest. It was comforting to him to do this, especially when he was forced to conduct nasty business, and lately he had been forced to conduct a lot of nasty business. 
                               *****
   An hour later, Lord Kint returned to the administrative centre feeling much more calm and focused. He summoned his General. 
   The aide was extremely agitated, "the General isn't available. I cannot reach him."
   "What do you mean?" demanded Kint, "you gave me that report yourself. The elves are religious fanatics. They refuse to work the mines, and they cry out for their Messiah. They even threaten to summon their god Corellon Larethian. They must be punished with military action. Five percent must die."
   Of course the aide knew all that, but he still hasn't been able to contact the General. 
   "Well then, who have you been able to contact?"
   The aide ran off to do whatever he could. He returned a few minutes later with a brand new report. Lord Kint took it from him roughly then quickly perused the contents. His grey face turned white. The elves would have to wait. Arik had made his move. The General was already making his way to the border with his best soldiers to defend Silver Land. Arik the half golem rebel had finally struck, his kodge army crossing the river. 
   The war had begun. See less

Part 62
Assassins among us!
1711 SD
   Assassins were among us!  Emperor Poul of the Zelred House knew that the Skulks were here. They hadn't been seen, but they had been felt. Every night one less noble had woken up. The Skulks were playing with him. 
   Emperor Poul decided to seal his personal rooms. Let no one in or out. What about food, and water? He could live upon conjured food and water. Conjured food was dry and fairly bland, but he would cope. And his stockpile of liqueur was within his chambers . 
   Emperor Poul of the Zelred was the true ruler of the Suel Imperium and nothing was going to stop him from fulfilling his destiny, and certainly not the magically created Skulks.
                                 *****
   Cenc saw Emperor Poul pouring himself a stiff drink. She saw him because she was in the room with him. She crouched on-top of a shelf of scrolls, unheard and unseen. A poisoned dagger was at her belt. He was sealing all of the doors. Even if he had beaten her to it,  closed off the rooms before the Skulks could get in, it wouldn't have saved him. The magician, Jaspi would have broken the locks. 
                                  *****
   Another false emperor eliminated. Another step closer to the end of the war. Why should the common soldiers die for the dreams of the elite? All of the Suel houses were fighting for the glory of the already glorious. Cenc was enjoying herself. The taking of lives of those that had never even seen her to look down on her was surprisingly easy. She supposed it was because she didn't see them as people. 
   The high Lords and Ladies, draped in red and white and gold, jostling for Themselves.
   They called themselves Suel and Human.
   Cenc was a Skulk. No longer a Suel, and no longer a human. She was an invisible assassin, as were all of her friends, murdering in order to save lives.
   Human lives. Suel lives.
   Cenc knew that she was a monster. It would be better for the Noble Houses to realise that they were only monsters too. See less

Part 63
A Funeral 
   Empress Gubudilana lay in her casket.  Bishop Nam-ko of the Order of Syrul supervised her placement into the golden carriage. The titanotheres were hitched up, and the procession was ready to begin.
   The Gargoyle Palace loomed above the mourners like a mountain. Somewhere within, Syrul was inside. Nam-ko turned to the Palace and bowed reverently. The blight that had befallen the Suel had even penetrated this holy place. The Skulks were everywhere, cowardly murderers who slew the good and dear. The greatest scions of the Imperium had vanished from the world. 
   Bishop Nam-ko bowed because she knew that Syrul was as appalled as she was. The goddess had chosen Gubudilana to rule the Imperium, but the cursed Wee Jas and her followers, corrupted by the impurity of the Zindians, would rather bring everything down than submit to the true Suel.
   The carriage began to move, the procession shuffling after it. With Empress Gubudilana gone, only one Emperor remained. The Emperor of the haunted Drow lands. The land of the betrayer, Wee Jas. Nam-ko returned to her position at the head of the crowd, her red gold symbol of a forked tongue raised so that everyone could see that Syrul was with them.
   The gravesite was beneath a natural slab of quartz surrounded by sweet smelling berry bushes. The hole had been dug, and two lesser clerics of Syrul waited there. The titanotheres pushed through thickets blocking the path, then the carriage emerged, bright and light on such a gloomy day. Bishop Nam-ko stepped forward to her comrades, and conversed with them briefly.  The titanotheres halted near the hole, then slaves brought down the casket, then carried it to the hole. As they gathered together the ropes and hoist, Nam-ko began the service.
   "How can this be?" she asked the mourners, "how can Syrul let our Imperium fall to the dark plots of Wee Jas?" Nam-ko paused, watching for reactions in the crowd. Many were sobbing, but others were yelling in anger, cursing Wee Jas and the Skulks.
   "Our Empress, Gubudilana of House Crix has indeed left us for her new journey," continued Nam-ko, "and with her death, the war is over."
   Cries of outrage. Roars of despair.
   "Hush, children, hush! Do you not yet understand the wisdom of Syrul? She herself will take Wee Jas to task. She herself has tasted the bitter salts of Wee Jas and her Zindia. The day dawns, shines and dims. The night shadows, glooms and glimmers. What is up comes down and what is down never forgets. Children, we are all Suel. Our day has darkened into night, and we have all fallen down. We lay the true Empress to rest, and we put away our arms. Calm shall return to the Imperium, and we must repose as our Empress must repose. But children, Suel, brothers and sisters of Syrul, we shall never forget who we are. We are of the Imperium and one day we will seize it utterly!" See less

Part 67
Under the Skin 
   The body that once belonged to Heward was finally breaking down. The hair was falling out, and what was left looked like white string. The face was cragged and going crooked, and the spine was bent. Wee Jas hadn't said anything, but Win-Daled the Suel Lich knew that she wasn't attractive to her anymore. Wee Jas was at the Palace less and less.
   It was time for Win-Daled to hunt for a new body. She hated the very thought of taking the life force of another person, but the hunger for life was gnawing away at her her from the inside. Who would she take? The younger and stronger the better, for a young body would last longer, and then she could defer the taking of another for quite some time. 
   A young convict, she decided. Some wastrel who had nothing but hatred in his heart. When she absorbed his life force, his evil would be discarded like a banana peel. She would discuss it with Wee Jas when she next returned. In the meantime, she would take care of herself with lots of sleep.
                               *****
   Win-Daled awoke in a foul mood. She lived down in the depths of the Palace so she had no idea of the time of the night or day. 
   She was hungry.
   That was odd. She seldom ate and taste meant nothing to her in any event. Perhaps her decaying body made her so? She rang for a servant. Wee Jas had several priestesses that lived here under the Palace, serving her small needs.    Baron Smoler had wanted to lead the attack upon Rhaan but his advisors cautioned against this. What if the city was better defended than expected, or what would become of the realm if by some freak chance, an arrow caught him in the throat or an eye? The fire giant infantry was the best in the world. Let them do their job.
   Smoler had agreed and now he regretted it. He had moved down into the Suel plains to get as close as possible without being drawn into the combat, and he quickly found that he couldn't see anything but the backs of the giants. The king had generously offered his Baron his personal guards of honour, and they were freaks, some reaching upward of eighteen feet high. Their armour was garish and ceremonial, and to make themselves even bigger their hats were heaped up masses of cave bear fur. They seemed barely trained with their great swords, holding them awkwardly, and their gangly bodies were shaped like stalks, and their square, elongated heads made them top heavy. 
   What made them far worse was that they completely blocked Smoler's view. He was ignominiously forced to retreat into the foothills where at least now he could see. Unfortunately, he felt incredibly distant from the melee unfolding below, and his dashing cloak of white furred snow serpent, his scale mail fashioned from hatchling silver dragons, and his mirrored sword seemed faintly ridiculous now. 
   The combatants might as well have been beetles or ants, so distant were they, but at least Smoler could make out the gist of the battle. It was going almost as well as he had expected, though one Suel magi and a few priests had bolstered the defenders (fortuitously only bringing down a couple of the King's guards) for a brief moment before being cut down. 
   Soon it was all over. His fire giants were victorious. The city fell to Baron Smoler.
                              *****
   Smoler entered the smouldering city and was at a loss of what to do with all of the Suel humans. Their were lots of old men, and boys, and thousands of women, girls and little children. Why hadn't they all fought like fire giants did when their halls were invaded? And they all chattered and yelped and wept with cries worse than giant goats. Smoler couldn't understand a word, but fortunately one of his advisors spoke Suel, and he was able to interpret.
   "They beg for their lives," said the advisor.
   "Do they think us barbarians?" exclaimed Smoler, "There is no honour in slaying non-combatants without good reason. Some we will take as slaves, of course. The rest...what do we do with them?"
   "We must organise them by sex. Males and females don't tend to like being heaped up all together. We should separate them and make them swear fealty to our King."
   Baron Smoler nodded in agreement.
